::: {.section-title}
Overview
:::

My research program sits at the intersection of applied and methodological work. On the applied side, I study the relationship between socioeconomic background and educational outcomes, particularly in secondary education and the transition to higher education in Chile. On the methodological side, I focus on the application and refinement of multilevel analysis and causal inference in educational research, with the goal of contributing to the development of statistical methods that accurately capture the complex relationships between educational outcomes and individual and contextual socioeconomic attributes.

::: {.section-title}
Applied Research
:::

Chilean research on educational outcomes consistently shows that students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds perform better on standardized tests. However, existing studies often overlook the nested nature of educational data — students within schools — leading to potential misinterpretations of individual and contextual effects. My work has contributed to this discussion by demonstrating the importance of considering both individual- and school-level factors when analyzing educational inequalities.

For instance, my studies on standardized tests such as SIMCE (used in secondary education) and university admission exams have revealed persistent score gaps linked to family income, parental education, and school dependency (private or public). These findings underscore the need for methodological approaches that can disentangle individual and contextual influences on student achievement.

::: {.section-title}
Methodological Research
:::

To address the challenges of analyzing clustered educational data, I apply and refine multilevel models, which allow for a more accurate estimation of educational inequalities. Despite their widespread use in social science research, multilevel models are challenging to specify correctly — particularly with respect to fixed and random effects. Recent studies suggest that misspecifications can lead to biased estimates, affecting how we interpret the role of student, family, and school characteristics in shaping educational outcomes.

My master's thesis in Educational Measurement and Statistics at the University of Iowa directly addresses this issue, examining how random slopes in multilevel models may conflate different sources of variance and lead to misleading conclusions about inter-cluster differences.

::: {.section-title}
Short-Term Goals
:::

- **Improve the methodological foundations of multilevel analysis** — clarify the consequences of incorrectly specifying fixed and random effects and develop guidelines for best practices in analyzing clustered educational data.

- **Bridge methodological advancements with applied research** — collaborate with interdisciplinary teams to analyze the relationship between educational segmentation and individual and school attributes in Chile and beyond.

::: {.section-title}
Long-Term Goals
:::

While much of my past work has centered on Chile, my broader interest lies in developing rigorous methodologies that can be applied across diverse educational systems. By refining statistical techniques and providing empirical evidence on the factors influencing student achievement, I aim to contribute to research that informs educational policy and promotes equity in learning opportunities.

As my career progresses, I remain open to different institutional contexts — whether in research-intensive universities or institutions that balance teaching and scholarship. My long-term goal is to engage in research that not only advances methodological rigor but also has practical implications for education policy and practice.
